title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

reading.body:
This is a false-positive match in an automated licence-plate recognition system, occurring at the point where a camera alert is handed to a patrol officer in the field. The system read one character of a plate incorrectly and returned a match to a stolen vehicle of the same make. The failure sits between the alert and the enforcement action, in the gap where a human is expected to confirm what the machine reported.

Catching it would have required the deputy to verify the plate against the vehicle in front of him before drawing a weapon, which is the check the vendor itself says the workflow assumes. The reported cause on the agency's side was a tinted plate cover, meaning the system was operating on input outside the conditions under which it reads reliably. That is a deployment question as much as a model question, since the same camera is expected to work on plates it cannot actually resolve.

What is not established is whether the plate cover was illegal, whether the deputy's conduct will be found reasonable by anyone other than his own office, and whether the misread was caused by the cover or by the reader. The sheriff's attribution and Flock's statement are both accounts given by interested parties, not findings.

reports.title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

summary: A York County, South Carolina, motorist, 42-year-old Steven Melvin, was reportedly held at gunpoint for over five minutes after a Flock Safety license-plate reader misread the first letter of his plate and matched his BMW to a similar stolen vehicle. The sheriff’s office later attributed the error to an illegal tinted plate cover, called the deputy’s actions reasonable, and Flock stated that alerts should be independently verified before enforcement.
